senses.sense_definition: Of, relating to, or containing electrically charged atoms or molecules (ions).

examples.text: Table salt dissolves in water to form an <w>ionic</w> solution containing sodium and chloride.
The students learned how an <w>ionic</w> bond forms between a metal and a nonmetal.

senses.sense_definition: Relating to one of the classical orders of Greek architecture, characterized by slender fluted columns and spiral scroll-like capitals.

examples.text: The ancient temple was supported by tall, elegant <w>Ionic</w> columns.
Architects frequently used the <w>Ionic</w> order when designing neoclassical government buildings.

senses.sense_definition: Of or relating to Ionia, an ancient region of western Asia Minor, or its people.

examples.text: Philosophers from various <w>Ionic</w> cities contributed significantly to early Greek thought.
Trade flourished throughout the region during the <w>Ionic</w> period.

senses.sense_definition: Of or relating to a style of heavy-faced printing type characterized by bracketed serifs.

examples.text: The vintage newspaper headline was set in an <w>Ionic</w> typeface to enhance legibility.
He preferred <w>Ionic</w> fonts for small print because the characters remained clear and sharp.

senses.sense_definition: A four-syllable metrical foot consisting of two short syllables followed by two long syllables, or vice versa, used in classical poetry.

examples.text: The poet carefully arranged each <w>ionic</w> to preserve the classical cadence of the verse.
Scholars identified an unusual <w>ionic</w> within the opening lines of the Latin poem.

senses.sense_definition: A subdialect of the Attic-Ionic dialect group of Ancient Greek, historically spoken in Ionia and parts of the Aegean.

examples.text: Herodotus wrote his famous historical accounts in an eastern variety of <w>Ionic</w>.
Linguists compare literary Attic with classical <w>Ionic</w> to trace changes in pronunciation.
